notes.meaning: God asks Job if he can catch Leviathan with an ordinary fishhook or tie a rope around its jaw. People often led tamed animals or carried fish by putting cords through their noses, but no human can do that to this beast. Most traditional interpreters see this creature as the mighty Nile crocodile.

other.label: Modern scholarship
other.view: Many scholars view Leviathan as a mythical sea monster from ancient Near Eastern stories that symbolizes chaos and evil, rather than an ordinary reptile.

notes.meaning: God asks whether this fierce creature would ever beg for mercy or speak soft words of surrender. A human captive might promise lifelong service to save his life, but Leviathan will never make an agreement to serve man.
People sometimes caught wild birds, put them in cages, or tied strings to their feet so young girls could play with them. God asks if Job could ever tame Leviathan to become a harmless family pet.
Fishermen and traders often caught fish together, divided up the meat, and sold it in the marketplace. God asks if merchants could ever capture Leviathan and barter for it like everyday goods.

Hunters could strike other water animals with harpoons, but Leviathan's skin is far too tough for spears to pierce. God warns that anyone who tries to lay a hand on this beast will remember the fight and never dare try it again.

Any thought of capturing or subduing this beast is completely empty. The mere sight of it is so terrifying that the boldest hunter will faint with fear. If no human has the courage to wake up God's creature, no one can possibly stand and challenge the Creator Himself.

God reminds Job that no one has ever given God anything first, so God owes nothing to anyone. Everything under heaven belongs to Him by right of creation. Since Job cannot claim that God is in his debt, he has no basis to demand a legal case against God.

differ.view: God owes no debt to any person, meaning human good works can never earn God's favor or obligate Him to save anyone.

notes.meaning: God announces that He will now describe the limbs, strength, and well-made body of Leviathan. Even in such a dangerous beast, the Lord takes note of its wonderful structure and power.
God asks who could ever peel back the creature's armored outer skin or dare reach into its mouth with a bridle. Its jaws open wide like heavy double doors, lined with a ring of terrifying teeth.

The beast's scales are its great pride, arranged in rows like shields locked firmly together. They fit so tightly against each other that not even air can pass between them. They grip one another so closely that no weapon can pry them apart.
When Leviathan snorts spray into the bright sunlight, the mist flashes like bursts of light. Its eyes emerging above the dark water glow brightly, like the first rays of the dawn.

The steam and breath rushing from the monster's mouth and nostrils are pictured as burning torches, smoke, and sparks. After holding its breath under water, the blast of hot vapor looks like steam from a boiling pot over a fire. This dramatic picture shows how terrifying the creature appears when it surfaces.
Tremendous physical strength has its home in the creature's thick neck. Terror and dismay seem to leap ahead of it, spreading panic wherever it moves.

The folds of its flesh and muscles are firmly knit together, leaving nothing loose or weak. Its heart and nature are solid as stone, as hard as the heavy lower millstone used to crush grain. It has no fear of danger and shows no pity.
When Leviathan rears up in the water, even the strongest warriors and sailors are gripped by terror. Its violent thrashing causes such confusion that the bravest men lose their footing and flee.
Swords and spears that strike the creature cannot penetrate its scales, often snapping on impact. Leviathan treats iron weapons like weak straw and bronze blades like rotten wood.
Arrows cannot drive the creature away, and heavy slingstones hit it like harmless bits of chaff. It treats wooden clubs like dry straw and simply laughs when a soldier brandishes a spear.

The scales covering the beast's underbelly are sharp and hard, like jagged pieces of broken pottery. When it lies down or crawls along the bank, it leaves deep tracks in the mud like a spiked threshing board.

As the creature thrashes through the deep water, it churns the river until it boils like a foaming pot of ointment. It leaves a bright, bubbling path behind it, making the deep waters look like the white hair of an aged man.

No beast on earth is equal to Leviathan, because it was created without any fear of man. It looks down on all other proud creatures as their undisputed king. By showing Job this untamable beast, God reminds him that only the Lord is truly sovereign over all things.

other.label: Catholic and Orthodox
other.view: Several early Christian teachers interpreted Leviathan as a symbol of Satan, the ruler of all proud spirits.
